newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries slump at sign of tight labor market.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries slump at sign of tight labor market.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended lower on Thursday after a sharp drop in weekly jobless claims figures underscored ongoing strength in the labor market.

The claims numbers lent the market a negative tone from the outset of trading and prices were unable to recover despite reports that the Federal Reserve was buying short-maturity Treasuries under the table for the second day in a row.
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond ended the day down 8/32 at 98-23/32 to yield 6.85 percent, while the 5.875 percent two-year note closed down 1/32 at 99-28/32 to yield 5.94 percent.
The U.S. Labor Department reported that initial state claims for unemployment benefits fell by a hefty 22,000 in the week ended October 19, registering 320,000 versus 342,000 in the previous period.
The claims total represented the lowest level for claims since they registered 317,000 in the week ended August 31.
The drop took Wall Street economists, who had forecast a claims total of 336,000 for the week, by surprise and served as a reminder that the U.S. labor market remains tight.

"We know the labor market is pretty strong and the claims number reminded us of that," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "It was a holiday week so the data might be a little tougher to read but there's no question that the labor market is still strong."

In addition to the Columbus Day holiday, economists said the ripple effects of the recently resolved strike by Canadian auto workers against General Motors Corp in Canada also may have had an impact on the data.
Regardless of any distortions, many said they expected claims to bounce back from their low levels next week.
With prices lingering in negative territory in the aftermath of the claims report, traders said the Fed entered the market, buying two-year, three-year and five-year paper.
"It looked like the Fed came in under the table once again and took the market off its lows," said Theodore Ake, senior vice president and senior trader at Everen Securities Corp.
However, Ake said the Fed-induced price rise was fleeting, giving the market little more than a temporary push up from session lows.
Further weighing on the market Thursday was ongoing apprehension about upcoming data. September durable goods orders are expected to rebound sharply from weak August numbers on Friday.
Meanwhile, widely divergent forecasts for the October employment report, due the following Friday, have also created some jitters in the market.
"I think there is a lot of nervousness and concern about next week's numbers," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
Three-month bill rates closed unchanged at 4.99 percent, six-month bill rates ended flat at 5.12 percent and year-bill rates rose one basis point to 5.26 percent.
The Treasury's new 6.25 percent five-year note ended down 3/32 at 99-25/32 to yield 6.30 percent and its 6.5 percent 10-year note closed down 5/32 to 99-15/32, yielding 6.57 percent.
